events.title: México City AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup|Nov 19 - Visualizing and Debugging Hugging Face's LeRobot Data|Online
events.description:
México City AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
This workshop is a hands-on tour of what actually breaks when you load real LeRobot datasets, and how Voxel51's native LeRobot support in FiftyOne catches it.

**Date, Time and Location**

Nov 19, 2026
9:00 AM - 10:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/lerobot-workshop-november-19-2026)**

Robot learning data doesn't look like the data that trains most vision-language models. It's temporal, low-dimensional in the parts that matter most, embodiment-specific, and expensive to collect, and increasingly, it's shipped in Hugging Face's LeRobot format. But packaging robot data consistently isn't the same as being able to see it: episodes hide broken metadata, silently dropped sensor modalities, and mismatched schemas between robots that look identical on paper.

Starting from the core differences that make robot data hard (temporal structure, proprioception, action grounding, embodiment heterogeneity, data scarcity), we'll move into live debugging: a metadata bug that broke multiple dataset imports, sensor streams that vanish without an error, and two robots running an identical benchmark whose data is structurally incompatible. By the end, you'll know what to check before you trust a LeRobot dataset, and how to actually look inside one.

Autonomous driving models rarely fail on the common case. They fail on the long-tail: the pedestrian stepping out from behind a parked truck or a construction zone that matches nothing in the training set. Each of those moments lives in synchronized multi-sensor data, made up of a LiDAR sweep, a ring of cameras, a timestamp, and a calibration. In this live session, we will take long-tail driving scenarios from discovery to 3D labels to evaluation, and make the case that 3D ground truth should be built where your data lives, not exported away from it.

**Your mAP is fine. Your slices are not. Finding the images that actually matter**

A single mAP can look acceptable while one slice is unusable, small objects, occlusion, or a confused class. I will run a pretrained detector on a few hundred public images (COCO-style, not a production crawl), report the headline metric, then break the same run by slice and walk through the worst samples.

The claim is modest: you do not need a million images or a trained-from-scratch model to see what the mean is hiding, and you cannot relabel everything, so the next labeling budget should follow those slices. No employer data and no confidential dashboards.

*About the Speaker*

[Amandeep Jiddewar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/amanfj/) is a Machine Learning Engineer at Pinterest, with prior work in U.S. manufacturing analytics (CertainTeed / Saint-Gobain) and marketplace allocation (QuinStreet). Emory Goizueta MSBA (2019), Kaggle Expert. This talk is in his personal capacity and does not represent his current or prior employers.

**Production AI Agents: Tool Use, Evaluation, Guardrails and Observability**

Building an AI agent is easy. Knowing whether it is behaving reliably in production is much harder. This session explores how to evaluate agents that use tools and external systems, including tool-call validation, tracing, observability, failure analysis, guardrails, permissions, and human review.

Attendees will learn practical patterns for understanding not just what an agent answered, but why it acted and whether the action was safe.

*About the Speaker*

[Akshay Talathi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/akshaytalathi/) is a Vice President at Goldman Sachs with over 10 years of experience building large-scale, cloud-native, and distributed systems across financial services and technology. His current focus is GenAI and agentic AI, including production AI agents, MCP, enterprise integrations, guardrails, observability, and reliable AI-driven workflows.

**From Virtual Worlds to Physical AI: Building Simulation Pipelines That Survive the Real World**

Robots are moving beyond perception systems that only detect and classify objects toward systems that must understand a scene, learn behaviors, and act in the physical world. In this talk, I’ll show a practical Physical AI workflow using OpenUSD, BowerBot, NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab to build a robot’s virtual world, including its body, cameras, sensors, and environment.

We’ll explore how demonstrations and reinforcement learning can teach behaviors in simulation, how vision and sensor data become observations for a robot policy, and what needs to match when transferring that behavior to real hardware. The demo follows a small robot from a simulated environment toward a real-world task, exposing both the power and the limitations of sim-to-real.

The goal is to make the path from pixels to actions concrete for computer vision and machine learning practitioners.

*About the Speaker*

[Arturo Morales Rangel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/arturo-morales-rangel) is the founder of Binary Core LLC, a Physical AI engineering company working across simulation, perception, robot learning, and deployment.

**Prompting Video-Language Models in Production: Lessons from Enterprise Video Tagging and Evaluation**

Video-language models can now describe, tag and answer questions about long-form video, but production results depend heavily on prompt design and evaluation. This talk shares field lessons from deploying such models for media, news, streaming and sports organizations, including how to structure prompts for consistent, schema-bound outputs across hours of footage.

On one sports video-tagging project, consolidating the prompt definitions cut estimated processing cost about 3x, and about 90% of the originally reported issues were later resolved through prompting alone. I'll also walk through building evaluation frameworks for video outputs, including for hard domains like egocentric video, and what changes when migrating between model versions.

Attendees will leave with reusable prompt patterns and an evaluation checklist they can apply to their own video pipelines.

*About the Speaker*

[Yash Gugale](https://www.linkedin.com/in/yashgugale/) is a Senior Forward Deployed Engineer at TwelveLabs in New York, integrating video foundation models (Marengo for embeddings and search, Pegasus for video-language understanding) for media, news, streaming and sports customers. He previously spent about six years in video streaming engineering at Peloton and Samsung TV Plus, and holds an MS in Computer Graphics Technology from Purdue.

events.description:
México City AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.

**Date, Time and Location**

Jan 14, 2027
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/mcp-agents-skills-meetup-january-14-2027)**

**From Demo to Production: Testing, Scaling and Securing AI Agents with Spring AI**

Your agent works perfectly in the demo. Then in production it gives a wrong answer and nobody can tell why, token costs spike, it slows to a crawl under load, and it calls a tool the user was never allowed to use. Building an agent is the easy part; the real work is running it like any other production service: tested, observable, scalable and secure.

Spring AI lets you do that with the Spring idioms and tooling you already know. This code-first session grows one example step by step. We start with a simple ChatClient, add advisors, memory and RAG, comparing the options Spring AI offers for each, and then let the agent act through tool calling and MCP.

Then come the production questions:

* Testing: we catch regressions with LLM-as-judge evaluators and typed decision models like Jev for fast, cheap verdicts.
* Observability: we add Micrometer traces, logs and token usage across model and tool calls.
* Scaling: we compare options for handling more concurrent users, from self-hosting to a managed runtime such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
* Security: we use Spring Security to authenticate users and make sure only the MCP tools they're allowed to use ever get called. You'll leave with reusable Spring patterns for agents that reason and act, and the discipline to test, observe, scale and secure them in production.

*About the Speaker*

[Andrei Shakirin](https://www.linkedin.com/in/andrei-shakirin/) is a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services and a former Pivotal Labs engineer, specializing in the design of highly scalable systems and generative AI applications. He is an active committer to several Spring and Apache open-source projects, contributor into MCP java SDK and a regular speaker at technical conferences.

**From Model Evals to System Evals: Evaluating Agents, Harnesses, and the Evaluators Themselves**

Every team shipping agents is quietly standing up two systems: the agent harness that plans, retrieves, calls tools, and edits code — and the evaluation harness that decides whether any of it can be trusted. Most teams only evaluate the first one's final output.

That is not enough. An agent can produce a correct answer through an unreliable, wasteful, or out-of-policy execution path, and outcome-only checks will pass it. This talk argues for evaluating the whole agent system: execution trajectories — tool correctness, evidence and grounding, state handling, policy compliance, and efficiency — alongside final outcomes, using deterministic specification checks an agent cannot game, model-based judges, and human-calibrated benchmarks.

We separate capability evaluations from regression evaluations so harness or model changes can be gated in CI. Then we turn the lens around: the evaluators themselves need evaluating — LLM judge calibration, disagreement analysis, and where human review still belongs.

Attendees leave with a production checklist for gating agent, model, and harness changes on system-level evidence instead of final answers.

*About the Speaker*

[Dipen Chawla](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dipen-chawla-bb4a49bb/) is an AI engineer and researcher working on agentic AI systems and their evaluation, including agent memory and clinical diagnostic reasoning work at Microsoft, and data platform engineering at Walmart and S&P Global.

**Leading an Army of AI Agents**

Our AI coding agents now pick up tasks, follow team playbooks, open pull requests and wait for review. This firsthand engineering case study follows more than ten agents running in parallel and shows how briefs, shared context and verification loops keep their work reviewable.
It covers the failure modes too: confident wrong turns, incomplete verification, review bottlenecks and the attention required from human leaders.
Attendees will learn a practical task-to-PR workflow, how to make trust conditional on evidence, and which measures expose the costs hidden by faster output. The focus is on agent workflow and operating discipline, with concrete engineering examples rather than a product pitch.

*About the Speaker*

[John Adib](https://www.linkedin.com/in/MrAdib) is a London-based engineering manager at Zapp, a former CTO and two-time founder with 18+ years of software experience.

Agents in Action: Putting AI Agents to Work on Visual AI Data

What should an AI agent remember, and what should it forget? In this talk, we’ll explore the Voxel51 agent through the lens of memory, examining how retaining the right context and incorporating feedback can help agents improve over time. Through examples from visual AI workflows, we’ll discuss what’s worth remembering, from dataset context and user preferences to corrections and successful approaches, and when to update or discard information that becomes outdated. We’ll also explore how feedback and evaluation can help us determine whether an agent is making better decisions, offering practical insights for building agents that become more useful with experience.

*About the Speaker*

[Adonai Vera](https://www.linkedin.com/in/adonai-vera/) is a Machine Learning Engineer and DevRel at Voxel51 with over 7 years of experience building computer vision and machine learning models using TensorFlow, Docker, and OpenCV.
